prime.problem: The bigram reads its logits straight out of a 65×65 table, so there is no per-token vector for later layers to work on. And the attention coming next mixes tokens without knowing their order: "tab" and "atb" would look the same to it.
prime.fits: This is the cleanup just before the crux. It rebuilds the bigram baseline out of the embedding lookups you met in makemore, and adds a second table for positions so that the self-attention card has something to tell order by.
prime.goal: Trace every shape from idx to logits, count the parameters, and explain why the position rows don't help this model yet but are essential once attention arrives.

attend: Why does the same character get a different x in slot 2 and slot 5, and which table causes the difference?
How can a (8, 32) tensor be added to a (32, 8, 32) tensor, and what does that imply about the 32 sequences in a batch?
If every prediction still comes from one character, what could a position row possibly add to the loss?
What exactly goes wrong if the model is handed 9 characters when block_size is 8?
Why does a content-based mixer need position rows when a fixed-order lookup like the bigram doesn't?

must: Token table row + position row are added into one C-wide x → the same character in two slots gets two different vectors → anything downstream that compares vectors can now tell slots apart

Attention scores tokens by content and sums them → swapping two earlier tokens just moves the same weights with them → the output is unchanged ("tab" = "atb") → the only order signal it gets is the position row added into x

The bigram model predicts from one token at a time → a position row can only say "I'm in slot t", not what came before → val loss doesn't improve (2.5163 vs 2.4903) → positions pay off only after tokens can talk
The position table has exactly block_size rows → there is no row for slot 8 → a 9-character input raises IndexError → generate() must crop the context to the last block_size characters
elevated: lm_head is a Linear layer with PyTorch's default init → the initial logits spread less (std 0.79 vs 1.01 for the 65×65 table) → the step-0 loss starts nearer the uniform 4.17 (4.48 vs bigram.py's 4.73)
reference: nanoGPT's names for the same tables: wte and wpe
the 2017 paper's fixed sinusoids, which it reports as nearly identical to learned rows

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the flow from idx to logits with every tensor's shape for B=32, T=8, C=32, then write 2–3 sentences on why the position table exists even though it doesn't lower this model's loss.
checklist: arange(8) → position table → pos_emb (8, 32), broadcast over the batch
one token per prediction, so positions add almost nothing yet
attention mixes tokens as a set, so the position row in x is its only source of order

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between what the token table stores and what the position table stores, and why their rows can be added rather than kept separate.
answer: token table: one learned row per character (65 rows), the same wherever it appears
position table: one learned row per slot (block_size rows), the same whatever character is there
both are trained together, so training decides how to share the 32 dimensions; adding keeps the width at C

retrieve.q: Walk one batch through forward: name each tensor and its shape, and say where broadcasting happens.
answer: tok_emb + pos_emb broadcasts pos_emb over the 32 sequences → x (32, 8, 32)
lm_head(x) → logits (32, 8, 65), then reshape to (256, 65) for cross-entropy

retrieve.q: gpt.py raises block_size from 8 to 256. What does that cost in the position table, and what does it buy and limit?
answer: 256 × 384 = 98,304 numbers, about four times the token table
every slot up to 256 gets its own learned row, so attention can use order over a longer context
still a hard limit: no row past slot 255, so longer inputs must be cropped

compare.q: The 65×65 bigram table vs token table + lm_head: both map one character to 65 logits. What is fundamentally different, and why is the version with a 32-number bottleneck the one to build on?
answer: bigram: the row is the logits; nothing sits between lookup and output
new: a C-wide vector sits in the middle, and later layers (attention, MLPs) can transform it
the bottleneck costs a little here (2.51–2.52 vs 2.49) but is what makes a deep model possible

compare.q: In makemore, the embedding C[X] fed a concatenated window into an MLP. Here each token gets its own vector plus a position row. Where did the position information live in makemore, and why can't the Transformer use the same trick?
answer: makemore: concatenation order fixed which slot each character's numbers occupied, so position was implicit
the Transformer keeps one vector per token and mixes them with order-blind attention
so position has to be written into each token's vector, by adding a position row

predict.q: Before attention, the average-the-past card mixed tokens with a plain average. If you add position rows to x and then take that plain average over "tab" and "atb", does the last token's average now differ between the two orders?
predict.answer: No. With the lab's seeded tables the difference is 1.2e-7, which is float noise. The average of (token + position) rows is the average of the three token rows plus the average of position rows 0–2, and both averages are the same in either order. Position rows only help when the weights depend on what sits in each slot, which is what queries and keys add on the next card.

apply.done: Your run ends at val loss 2.5123 (vs 2.5163 with the add), and you can say why the position rows don't matter to a model that only sees one character per prediction.
